key: # Written by the assistant and NOT CHECKED AGAINST A SOURCE. Every one is a
# claim a person should either confirm or replace. The register is honest
# about its coordinates being authored; this is the same admission about its
# prose. Overwrite freely — that is what the column is for.
# The sentence answers ONE question: what about this ground
name: or this thing on
decided something. Not what it was — the `kind` column says that.
Athenae
why: The city itself: a defensible rock with a spring, a plain behind it for grain, and a bay six miles off deep enough for a fleet. Few places in Greece have all three.

name: Agora of Athens
why: Market, law court, mint and meeting place on one patch of level ground below the Acropolis — the only large flat space inside the walls, and so the place the city did everything in public.

name: Dipylon Gate
why: The main gate, where the road from Eleusis and the Panathenaic procession both entered. A double gate with a courtyard: an enemy through the first was trapped under the walls.

name: Kerameikos
why: The potters' quarter outside the wall, and the state burial ground. Athens put its dead and its kilns on the same downwind side of the city.

name: Stoa Poikile
why: A painted colonnade on the Agora's north side. Zeno taught under it and his followers were named for the porch rather than for him.

name: Pnyx
why: A hillside cut into a bowl facing the city, where the assembly met. The speaker stood with the Acropolis behind the crowd — a democracy that voted in the open air, in sight of what it was voting about.

name: Areopagus
why: The bare rock west of the Acropolis where the oldest council sat, and later the homicide court. High enough to see the Agora and separate from it.

name: Academy/Akademeia/Akademia
why: An olive grove and gymnasion a mile outside the walls, watered by the Kephisos. Plato taught there because it was public ground with shade and water, not because it was his.

name: Lyceum
why: The other gymnasion, east of the city, where Aristotle walked while teaching. Two schools on opposite sides of one small city.

name: Panathenaic Way
why: The processional road from the Dipylon Gate through the Agora and up to the Acropolis. The one route the whole city walked together, and the reason the Agora is shaped as it is.

name: Panathenaic Stadium
why: A natural ravine between two hills, adapted rather than built — the ground gave the seating and the track its length.

name: Theater of Dionysus Eleuthereus
why: Cut into the south slope of the Acropolis, so the hill carried the seats and the audience faced the sea. Tragedy was performed here first.

name: Parthenon
why: Built on the Acropolis rock over the burnt foundations of an earlier temple the Persians destroyed in 480 BC. The ruin was left visible for a generation before it was replaced.

name: Erechtheion
why: Built around older things that could not be moved — the salt spring, the olive, the tomb. Its awkward plan is the ground refusing to be levelled.

name: Kantharos Limen
why: The commercial harbour of Piraeus and the largest of the three. Grain from the Black Sea and Egypt came ashore here, and Athens could be starved by closing it.

name: Zea Limen
why: The main naval harbour, ringed with ship-sheds — close to two hundred slipways cut into the rock, where the trireme fleet was drawn out of the water between campaigns.

name: Mounichia Limen
why: The smallest and most defensible of the three Piraeus harbours, under the hill fort. A fleet could be held here when the city could not hold the others.

name: Phaleron
why: The open beach Athens used before Piraeus was fortified. Ships were run up the sand rather than moored, which is why Themistokles moved the fleet.

name: Marathon
why: A coastal plain with marsh at both ends, so a landing force had to fight on a front the ground chose. The Athenians held the high edge and closed it.

name: Salamis (island)
why: The island that makes the Saronic Gulf a set of channels rather than open water. A fleet lured into the strait could not use its numbers, and in 480 BC the Persian fleet was.

name: Eleusis
why: The sanctuary of the Mysteries, on the bay at the end of the Sacred Way. Twenty kilometres from Athens — near enough to walk in procession, far enough to be its own place.

name: Laureion
why: The silver. The hills south of Athens held argentiferous lead, and the fleet that fought at Salamis was paid for out of a single rich strike in 483 BC.

name: Thorikos
why: The port and processing site for the Laureion mines, with washeries for the ore and the earliest surviving Greek theatre — an industrial town that could afford one.

name: Rhamnous
why: A fortress on the cliff above the Euboean strait, watching the sea road that grain convoys used to reach Athens from the north.

name: Eleutherai
why: A fort in the pass over Kithairon between Attica and Boeotia — the land route an army from Thebes had to take.

name: Dekeleia
why: High ground overlooking the Athenian plain and the road to Euboea. Sparta fortified it in 413 BC and Athens lost the use of her own countryside for the rest of the war.

name: Delphi
why: A terrace on the cliffs of Parnassus where the oracle sat, reachable from every Greek state and belonging to none. Its neutrality was a fact of geography before it was a policy.

name: Corinthus/Korinthos
why: The city on the isthmus, holding the only land route into the Peloponnese and two harbours on two seas. Whoever held Corinth decided who moved.

name: Thebai/Thebae
why: The chief city of the Boeotian plain, on the flat ground an army from the north crosses to reach Attica. Athens and Thebes fought over the passes between them for two centuries.

name: Megara
why: Between Athens and Corinth on the coast road, with mountains behind. Small, and unavoidable — which is why an Athenian trade embargo on it helped start a war.

name: Aigina (settlement)
why: An island in plain sight of the Athenian coast, with its own fleet. Perikles is said to have called it the eyesore of the Piraeus, and Athens took it.

name: Argos
why: The old power of the Argive plain, the best farmland in the Peloponnese, and Sparta's nearest rival for it.

name: Sparta
why: An unwalled city on the Eurotas, ringed by mountains that did the work walls do elsewhere. Its defence was the ground and the men, in that order.

name: Chalcis
why: On the Euripos, the narrowest crossing to Euboea, where the current reverses several times a day. A bridge here joins the island to the mainland.

name: Oropos
why: The port facing Euboea, disputed between Athens and Thebes for centuries because whoever held it controlled the short crossing to the island's grain.

name: Amphiareion
why: A healing sanctuary in a wooded ravine near Oropos, where the sick slept for a dream. Its remoteness was the treatment.

name: Brauron/sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia
why: A sanctuary on the marshy east coast where Athenian girls served Artemis before marriage. Far from the city on purpose.

name: Thermopylae
why: A strip between cliff and sea, and in 480 BC the only road south into Greece for an army. THE COAST HAS SILTED SIX KILOMETRES SINCE — the pass is in the terrain, the narrowness is not.

name: Aphrodite sanctuary at Dafni
why: On the Sacred Way between Athens and Eleusis, where the procession halted. A Christian monastery was later built on the same spot for the same reason: everyone passed it.

Krete
why: The long island closing the Aegean from the south, far enough offshore to develop its own power and near enough to be fought over. Invisible to this register until the corpus was asked in Latin.

name: Peloponnesus/Peloponnesos/Peloponnese
why: The peninsula behind the isthmus — an army that got past Corinth was inside, and one that did not was outside. Athenian strategy for thirty years was a argument about that neck of land.

name: Lacedaemon/Laconia
why: The Eurotas valley behind Taygetos and Parnon, farmed by a subject population. The mountains that made Sparta safe also made her unable to leave for long.

name: Olympos (mountain)
why: The highest ground in Greece, at the northern edge of it, permanently in cloud. A mountain nobody lived on became the address of the gods.

name: Hellas (Late Roman province)
why: Not a state but a name a scatter of rival cities agreed to answer to. The word does more work in the corpus than any city in it.

name: Isthmos
why: Four miles of land between two seas. It carried the road south, the drag-way for ships, the games, and every congress at which the Greek states tried to act as one.

name: Euboea (island)
why: The long island shielding the eastern coast, and Athens' nearest grain and cattle ground. When Euboea revolted the city felt it faster than a defeat abroad.

name: Attica
why: The peninsula itself: thin soil, good stone, silver in the south, and a coastline with more harbours than farmland. A country that had to trade to eat.

name: Apollonia
why: A port on the far Adriatic shore where a Roman army crossing from Italy came ashore. Caesar wintered against it; Octavian was studying there when Caesar died.

name: Helena (island)
why: The bare strip off the east coast on the Aegean crossing, named for a landfall in the Helen story. A sea-mark before it was ever a place.

name: Artemis Tauropolos temple
why: A sanctuary at Halai Araphenides on the east coast, facing the sea the Tauric legend comes across. Sited where a ship from the Black Sea would land.

name: Acropolis of Athens
why: The rock: a spring, one approachable side, and a summit large enough to hold a citadel. Every Athenian century built on top of the last one here.

name: Tholos at the Sanctuary of Asklepios, Epidauros
why: A round building at the healing sanctuary, on ground reached only by a day's journey. The distance was part of the cure and the sanctuary's income.

name: A(n)thene
why: A small Kynourian town on the disputed border ground between Argos and Sparta. Its name is close enough to Athens to be a trap for a name-matcher.

name: Anthedon
why: The last harbour on the Boeotian coast before the Euripos narrows, a fishing port on the strait a fleet had to pass.

name: Aegina (island)
why: The island in the middle of the Saronic Gulf, in sight of both Athens and the Peloponnese, minting silver before Athens did.

name: Kaukasos (mountain)
why: The eastern wall of the known world, where Prometheus was chained. Its use in the corpus is as a limit, not a location.

name: Hydroussa/Hydrea (island)
why: A waterless rock off the Argolid whose name means the watered one. The harbour was the whole reason for the settlement.

name: Patroklou Charax (island)
why: The island off Sounion fortified as a naval station, named for the admiral who entrenched on it. A blockade of Athens starts here.

name: Doris
why: A few villages in the mountains above Phocis, and the claimed homeland of the Dorians. Sparta went to war to defend a place of no value but great genealogy.

name: Marios
why: A minor Laconian settlement. IT IS ALSO A TRAP: the derived form is Marius, and seven rooms name the Roman general, not this ground.

name: Pyra
why: The pyre-sanctuary on Oita where Herakles was said to have burned. A cult sited on a mountain-top because the story required height and fire.

name: Arcadia
why: The high interior of the Peloponnese, poor and mountainous, which supplied the rest of Greece with mercenaries and later with a pastoral fiction.

name: Boeotia
why: The wide plain north of Kithairon — the best cavalry ground near Attica and the corridor any northern army uses. Athens' history is largely the passes into it.

name: Peiraieus/Piraeus
why: The rock peninsula with three natural harbours that Themistokles walled and made the city's seaward half. Athens then built long walls so the two could not be separated.

name: Orchestra in the Agora of Athens
why: The dancing floor in the Agora where performances were held before the theatre was cut into the Acropolis slope. The city's first audience space was its market.

name: Hermion(e)
why: A port on the Argolic peninsula with deep water close inshore, and a cult of Demeter drawing traffic that the harbour then held.

name: Dionysos, T.
why: A temple of the god whose festival carried the drama. Where his precinct stood, the theatre followed.

name: Cyclades Islands
why: The ring of islands that makes the Aegean crossable in day-stages. Whoever held them held the route, which is what the Athenian empire was.

name: Tegea
why: The Arcadian city on the road north out of Laconia. Sparta needed it friendly to march at all, and bound it by treaty rather than conquest.

name: Mysia (settlement)
why: A settlement carrying a name that belongs mostly to Asia Minor — a place the corpus reaches for when it means somewhere east.

name: Eileithyaia, Zeus Hypatos, Aphrodite?, T.
why: A shared precinct where three cults sat on one patch of ground. Space inside a city walls was scarcer than piety.

name: Megalopolis
why: A city founded from scratch after Leuktra to hold the Arcadian plain against Sparta. A settlement built as a strategy.

name: Parnassus (mountain)
why: The mountain above Delphi, whose cliffs give the oracle its terrace and its inaccessibility. The sanctuary is where it is because the mountain stops there.

name: Pelion (mountain)
why: The wooded ridge above the Magnesian coast, timber for ships and the schoolroom of the centaur. A mountain the corpus goes to for wood and for stories.

name: Akyphas/Pindos
why: On the range that divides Thessaly from Epirus — the watershed that decides which sea a river reaches, and which way an army can go.

name: Plataea
why: The Boeotian town under Kithairon that stayed with Athens, and so the ground where the Persian war ended in 479 BC. It was destroyed twice for the choice.

name: Aphidna
why: A deme in the northern hills with its own acropolis, where Theseus was said to have hidden Helen. Far enough from Athens to be a hiding place.

name: Trachis/Herakleia
why: The town behind Thermopylae, on the only ground an army holding the pass can camp. Sparta refounded it to control the road.

name: Basilica
why: A hall type that arrives with Rome and puts the law court under a roof. Where one stands, the Greek open-air assembly has already ended.

name: Euripos
why: The strait at Chalcis where the current reverses several times a day, forty metres wide. A fleet has to time it, and an army can bridge it.

name: Phthiotis
why: The Achilles country in southern Thessaly. The corpus names it for a man rather than for anything on the ground.

name: Chaeronea
why: The plain at the western entrance to Boeotia where a northern army debouches. Philip destroyed the Greek city-states' independence on it in 338 BC.

name: Cephisus (river)
why: The Boeotian river that drains into Lake Kopais with no outlet to the sea — which is why the plain floods and why draining it was worth an empire's effort.

name: Leuktra
why: Flat ground in Boeotia where Epaminondas broke the Spartan line in 371 BC and ended the belief that it could not be broken.

name: Pnyx fountain
why: The Kallirrhoe spring below the Pnyx, one of the few reliable waters inside the city. Athens sited its assembly next to its drinking water.

name: Skotoussa (Thessaly)
why: A Thessalian town on the ridge road, near the Kynoskephalai hills where the phalanx lost to the legion in 197 BC.

name: Temple of Nemesis
why: The sanctuary at Rhamnous above the strait, whose cult statue was said to be cut from marble the Persians brought for their victory monument.

name: Thisbe
why: A small Boeotian town on the Corinthian gulf side of Helicon, reached by a pass. Its harbour is separated from it by the mountain.

name: Selinous
why: A river-name repeated across the Greek world for the celery on its banks. The corpus names the water, not always this one.

name: Erineos
why: A Doris village, and a shore on the Corinthian gulf where a fleet was beached. Two claims on one name.

name: Paneion (mountain)
why: A hill with a cave of Pan north of the city, in the sort of high goat ground the god was believed to keep.

name: Malea
why: The cape at the south-east corner of the Peloponnese, where the winds meet. Ancient sailors preferred to drag ships over the isthmus than round it.

name: Peparethus (island)
why: A Sporades island growing wine, on the northern Aegean route out to Thrace and the Hellespont.

name: Siphnos (settlement)
why: A Cycladic island with gold and silver mines rich enough to pay a tithe at Delphi, until the sea broke into the workings.

name: Aegaeum Mare
why: The sea itself: shallow, island-strewn, and crossable by day-stages, which is why Greek power was naval and dispersed rather than territorial.

name: Castalian spring
why: The spring at Delphi where pilgrims washed before consulting. The sanctuary's practical requirement and the reason it sits at that height on the cliff.

name: Helike
why: The Achaean city on the gulf swallowed by an earthquake and the sea in 373 BC, with the whole population lost. The corpus keeps it as a warning.

name: Pallene
why: A deme on the road from the east coast into Athens, where Peisistratos beat the city's levy and took the tyranny.

name: Taygetos (mountain)
why: The wall west of Sparta: a barrier to Messenia that had to be crossed to hold the subject ground on the other side.

name: Helicon (mountain)
why: The mountain the Muses were given, above Askra where Hesiod farmed. The Greek image of poetry starts from a real and poor hillside.

name: Inachos (river)
why: The river of the Argive plain, dry most of the year. Argos' claim to its own antiquity runs through a watercourse that is usually a bed.

name: Messene
why: The city built under Ithome after Leuktra to make Messenia permanently free of Sparta — and so to halve Sparta's farmland.

name: Munychia
why: The hill above the smallest Piraeus harbour, and the fort that commanded all three. Every faction that took Athens took this hill first.

name: Palladion
why: The court that tried unintentional homicide, named for the image it held. Athens gave each degree of killing its own ground.

name: Phleious
why: A small independent city on the plateau between Corinth, Sicyon and Argos, holding a road junction it was too weak to close.

name: Phocis
why: The region around Delphi, whose people repeatedly seized the sanctuary they lived beside. Proximity to a neutral shrine is not neutrality.
